meta.note: Batch 1 of ~7 toward the 350-question v1 target. All items authored clean-room from primary sources (statutes, regulations, and the public NMLS Test Content Outline). Each item carries a primary_source_citation. Requires SME + legal review before commercial use. Figures reflect general/commonly-tested values; verify current thresholds at each quarterly review.
meta.id_note: Question ids are opaque; content_area and outline_ref are authoritative (the id prefix is not).

questions.stem: A settlement agent offers an MLO $250 for each closed loan the MLO refers, with no service performed in exchange. Under RESPA, this arrangement is:
options: Permissible if the borrower is told about it in writing
A prohibited referral fee subject to criminal penalties
Permissible because settlement services are involved
Permissible if the payment stays under $500 per loan
questions.explanation: RESPA Section 8(a) prohibits giving or accepting any fee, kickback, or thing of value for referring settlement-service business. A payment tied purely to referrals, with no compensable service rendered, is exactly the conduct banned, and it carries criminal exposure (fines up to $10,000 and up to one year in prison). Disclosure to the borrower does not cure a Section 8 violation, the presence of settlement services does not make a referral fee legal, and there is no dollar-amount safe harbor that permits it.
questions.primary_source_citation: 12 U.S.C. §2607(a), (d); Regulation X, 12 CFR §1024.14

questions.stem: A consumer closes on a loan to purchase their primary residence and, two days later, wants to cancel under the right of rescission. What is the correct response?
options: They may cancel by the end of the third business day
The right of rescission does not apply to a purchase-money loan
They may cancel within three years
They may cancel only if the appraisal was late
questions.explanation: The TILA right of rescission does not extend to residential mortgage (purchase-money) transactions secured by the consumer's principal dwelling. It applies to refinances with a new creditor, home-equity lines, and home-improvement loans on the principal dwelling. Because this is a purchase, there is no three-business-day or three-year rescission right, and the appraisal timing is irrelevant to whether rescission applies.
questions.primary_source_citation: 15 U.S.C. §1635(e); Regulation Z, 12 CFR §1026.23(a), (f)

questions.stem: On a refinance of a principal residence with a new creditor, the lender never delivered the notice of the right to rescind. How long may the consumer have to rescind?
options: Three business days from consummation, regardless
Up to three years, because required notice/disclosures were not provided
Thirty days from the first payment
There is no rescission right on a refinance
questions.explanation: When the lender fails to deliver the notice of the right to rescind or the material TILA disclosures, the rescission window extends from three business days to as long as three years. The three-business-day period assumes proper delivery, so it does not control here. The thirty-day option is a distractor drawn from ECOA timing, and a new-creditor refinance of a principal dwelling is in fact rescindable.

questions.stem: Once a consumer submits the six items that constitute an application, the Loan Estimate must be delivered or placed in the mail no later than:
options: At consummation
Three business days after receiving the application
Three business days before consummation
Thirty days after application
questions.explanation: The Loan Estimate must be delivered or mailed within three business days of receiving an application. The 'three business days before consummation' option is the Closing Disclosure rule, a frequently tested trap. Delivering at consummation is far too late, and thirty days is an ECOA notice period, not a TRID disclosure deadline.
questions.primary_source_citation: Regulation Z, 12 CFR §1026.19(e)(1)(iii)

questions.stem: The consumer must receive the Closing Disclosure no later than:
options: Three business days after application
Three business days before consummation
On the day of closing
Within thirty days of the Loan Estimate
questions.explanation: The consumer must receive the Closing Disclosure at least three business days before consummation, allowing time to compare final terms to the Loan Estimate. Certain changes, such as an APR increase beyond tolerance, addition of a prepayment penalty, or a change in loan product, restart that three-day clock. The other options confuse this with the Loan Estimate deadline or invent timeframes.
questions.primary_source_citation: Regulation Z, 12 CFR §1026.19(f)(1)(ii)

questions.stem: Under ECOA, notice of adverse action on a completed application must be provided within:
options: 3 business days
15 days
30 days
60 days
questions.explanation: ECOA and Regulation B require notice of adverse action within 30 days after receiving a completed application. The same 30-day framework governs notices of approval, counteroffers, and incompleteness. The three-business-day option borrows from TILA disclosure timing; 15 and 60 days are not the ECOA standard.
questions.primary_source_citation: 15 U.S.C. §1691(d); Regulation B, 12 CFR §1002.9(a)(1)

questions.stem: Which loan feature would disqualify a loan from Qualified Mortgage status?
options: A 30-year fixed term
Points and fees of 2.5% of the loan amount
Negative amortization
Full verification of income and assets
questions.explanation: A Qualified Mortgage may not include negative amortization, interest-only payments, balloon payments (with limited exceptions), terms exceeding 30 years, or points and fees above the applicable cap (generally 3%). A 30-year term is allowed, 2.5% in points and fees is under the cap, and verifying income and assets is a requirement for a QM rather than a disqualifier.
questions.primary_source_citation: Regulation Z, 12 CFR §1026.43(e)

questions.stem: Under the Ability-to-Repay rule, how many underwriting factors must a creditor consider?
options: Three
Five
Eight
Twelve
questions.explanation: The ATR rule requires creditors to consider eight underwriting factors, including current income or assets, employment status, the monthly mortgage payment, payments on simultaneous loans, other mortgage-related obligations, current debt and alimony/child support, the monthly debt-to-income ratio or residual income, and credit history. The other counts are distractors.
questions.primary_source_citation: Regulation Z, 12 CFR §1026.43(c)(2)

questions.stem: On the Uniform Residential Loan Application (Form 1003), which section captures the borrower's basic identifying information, such as name and Social Security number?
options: Section 1: Borrower Information
Section 4: Loan and Property Information
Section 5: Declarations
Section 8: Demographic Information
questions.explanation: Section 1 collects borrower identifying and employment/income information. Section 4 covers loan and property details, Section 5 is declarations (such as bankruptcy or pending lawsuits), and Section 8 gathers demographic data for fair-lending monitoring. Knowing which URLA section holds which content is frequently tested in the origination area.
questions.primary_source_citation: Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac Uniform Residential Loan Application (Form 1003/65), Section 1

questions.stem: A borrower declines to provide the ethnicity, sex, and race information in Section 8 of the URLA during a face-to-face application. The MLO should:
options: Refuse to continue until the borrower answers
Note that the borrower declined and record the information by visual observation or surname as required
Leave the application incomplete and stop working on it
Enter assumptions and treat them as borrower-supplied facts
questions.explanation: Section 8 demographic data supports HMDA and fair-lending monitoring. Borrowers may decline, but for applications taken in person the MLO must still note the information on the basis of visual observation or surname. The MLO never refuses the application over this, never treats it as a stopping point, and never records assumptions as if the borrower supplied them.
questions.primary_source_citation: Regulation C, 12 CFR §1003.4(a)(10); Appendix B to Part 1003

questions.stem: A property appraises at $250,000 and the borrower finances $200,000. The loan-to-value ratio is:
questions.explanation: Loan-to-value equals the loan amount divided by the property value (the lesser of sale price or appraised value): $200,000 / $250,000 = 0.80, or 80%. On a conventional loan, 80% LTV is the threshold at or below which private mortgage insurance is typically avoided.
questions.primary_source_citation: Standard mortgage underwriting definition; see Regulation Z §1026.32 for LTV usage in high-cost tests

questions.stem: Gross monthly income is $6,000. The proposed housing payment is $1,500 and other monthly debts total $600. The back-end (total) DTI is:
questions.explanation: Back-end DTI equals total monthly debt, including housing, divided by gross monthly income: ($1,500 + $600) / $6,000 = $2,100 / $6,000 = 35%. The 25% figure is the front-end (housing-only) ratio and is offered as a distractor.
questions.primary_source_citation: Standard underwriting definition; DTI referenced in Regulation Z §1026.43(c)(7)

questions.stem: A borrower pays 2 discount points on a $180,000 loan. In dollars, that equals:
questions.explanation: One discount point equals 1% of the loan amount. Two points is 2% of $180,000: 0.02 × $180,000 = $3,600. Points are prepaid interest paid at closing to reduce the note rate.
questions.primary_source_citation: Standard mortgage-finance definition; points treated as prepaid finance charge under Regulation Z §1026.4

questions.stem: Per-diem (prepaid) interest collected at closing covers:
options: Interest from the disbursement date through the end of that month
Interest for the entire first year of the loan
The lender's origination fee
Interest during the rescission period only
questions.explanation: Because mortgage interest is paid in arrears, per-diem interest at closing covers the days from disbursement through the last day of that month. Closing later in the month reduces the prepaid interest collected. It is not a full year of interest, is unrelated to the origination fee, and is not limited to the rescission period.
questions.primary_source_citation: Standard closing-cost practice; prepaid interest disclosed on the Closing Disclosure, Regulation Z §1026.38

questions.stem: Which set of items constitutes an application under TRID, triggering the Loan Estimate deadline?
options: Name, income, Social Security number, property address, estimated property value, and loan amount sought
Only a signed purchase contract
Name and phone number
A completed appraisal and title commitment
questions.explanation: TRID defines an application by six pieces of information: name, income, Social Security number, property address, estimated property value, and the loan amount sought. Receiving all six starts the three-business-day Loan Estimate clock. A purchase contract, contact details alone, or third-party reports do not by themselves constitute an application.
questions.primary_source_citation: Regulation Z, 12 CFR §1026.2(a)(3)

questions.stem: An application arrives missing information needed to make a credit decision. The proper action is to:
options: Deny the loan immediately for incompleteness
Send a notice of incompleteness stating what is needed and a reasonable deadline
Wait indefinitely for the borrower to follow up
Approve conditionally and gather documents after closing
questions.explanation: For an incomplete application, Regulation B provides for a notice of incompleteness that specifies the information required and sets a reasonable time to supply it, generally within the 30-day framework. An outright denial for incompleteness, indefinite inaction, or closing first and collecting later are all improper.
questions.primary_source_citation: Regulation B, 12 CFR §1002.9(c)

questions.stem: On an adjustable-rate mortgage, the fully indexed rate equals:
options: Index minus margin
Index plus margin
Margin minus the lifetime cap
Start rate plus the periodic cap
questions.explanation: The fully indexed rate is the index plus the margin. The index moves with the market, while the margin is the lender's fixed add-on that remains constant for the life of the loan. Caps then limit how much the rate may actually change at each adjustment and over the loan's life.
questions.primary_source_citation: Standard ARM definition; ARM disclosure requirements at Regulation Z §1026.19(b) and §1026.20(c)

questions.stem: An ARM is quoted as '2/2/5.' The middle number represents the:
options: Initial adjustment cap
Periodic (subsequent) adjustment cap
Lifetime cap
Margin
questions.explanation: In a 2/2/5 structure the first number is the initial adjustment cap, the middle number is the periodic cap limiting each subsequent adjustment, and the final number is the lifetime cap over the start rate. The margin is a separate figure and is not one of the three cap numbers.
questions.primary_source_citation: Standard ARM cap convention; consumer ARM booklet referenced in Regulation Z §1026.19(b)

questions.stem: Which statement about FHA loans is correct?
options: They require a 20% down payment
They require mortgage insurance (upfront plus annual) regardless of down payment
They are available only to veterans
They never require mortgage insurance
questions.explanation: FHA loans permit low down payments but require mortgage insurance, an upfront premium plus an annual premium, which on most current terms lasts the life of the loan. They are not limited to veterans (that describes VA loans), do not require 20% down, and always carry FHA mortgage insurance.
questions.primary_source_citation: National Housing Act; HUD FHA Single Family Handbook 4000.1

questions.stem: A defining feature of a VA loan is:
options: A required 10% down payment
No down payment for eligible borrowers and a funding fee in place of monthly mortgage insurance
Mandatory monthly private mortgage insurance
Availability to any borrower regardless of service
questions.explanation: VA loans allow eligible veterans and service members to purchase with no down payment and charge a one-time funding fee instead of monthly mortgage insurance. They are limited to those with qualifying military service and certain eligible survivors, and they do not carry monthly PMI.
questions.primary_source_citation: 38 U.S.C. Chapter 37; VA Lenders Handbook (VA Pamphlet 26-7)

questions.stem: A loan whose amount exceeds the conforming loan limits set by the FHFA is called a:
options: FHA loan
Conforming loan
Jumbo (non-conforming) loan
Bridge loan
questions.explanation: Loans above the FHFA conforming limits cannot be purchased by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac and are called jumbo, or non-conforming, loans. They typically carry stricter underwriting because they lack GSE backing. A bridge loan is short-term interim financing and is unrelated to loan size limits.
questions.primary_source_citation: Federal Housing Finance Agency conforming loan limit definitions (12 U.S.C. §1717)

questions.stem: Negative amortization occurs when:
options: The borrower pays extra toward principal each month
The payment is less than the interest due, so unpaid interest is added to principal
The loan is paid off early
The rate is fixed for the life of the loan
questions.explanation: Negative amortization means the periodic payment does not cover the interest owed, so the shortfall is added to the loan balance and the borrower can owe more over time than originally borrowed. It is a prohibited feature for Qualified Mortgages. The other options describe accelerated payoff, early payoff, or a fixed rate.
questions.primary_source_citation: Regulation Z, 12 CFR §1026.43(e)(2)(i); definition at §1026.18(s)

questions.stem: A borrower says their real income is lower than what would qualify them and asks the MLO to enter a higher figure. The MLO should:
options: Enter the higher figure because the borrower requested it
Refuse to falsify income and record only accurate, verifiable information
Enter the higher figure but label it an estimate
Average the two figures
questions.explanation: Overstating income is loan fraud regardless of who requests it. The MLO must record only accurate, verifiable information. Entering a false figure, disguising it as an estimate, or averaging toward a false number all constitute falsification and expose the MLO to license revocation and criminal liability.
questions.primary_source_citation: SAFE Act prohibited acts, 12 CFR §1008.103; general fraud prohibitions

questions.stem: A caller who is not a party to the loan asks the MLO for details about a borrower's application. The MLO should:
options: Share the information since the caller seems to know the borrower
Decline to disclose the borrower's nonpublic personal information to outside parties
Share only the loan amount
Confirm whether the person has applied
questions.explanation: Borrower application information is nonpublic and protected. The MLO must not disclose details, or even confirm that someone has applied, to unauthorized outside parties. Sharing a partial detail like the loan amount, or confirming the existence of an application, still breaches the duty to safeguard customer information.
questions.primary_source_citation: Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act privacy provisions, 15 U.S.C. §6801; Regulation P, 12 CFR Part 1016

questions.stem: An MLO could earn more by placing a well-qualified borrower into a costlier subprime product the borrower does not need. Doing so would be:
options: Acceptable if the borrower agrees
Steering, which is a prohibited practice
Required to maximize lender revenue
Permitted if disclosed on the Loan Estimate
questions.explanation: Directing a borrower into a worse or costlier loan than they qualify for, to increase the originator's compensation, is steering, which the Loan Originator Compensation rule and fair-lending principles prohibit. Borrower consent or a disclosure does not make steering acceptable.
questions.primary_source_citation: Regulation Z, 12 CFR §1026.36(e) (anti-steering)

questions.stem: While reviewing bank statements, an MLO notices a large deposit inconsistent with the borrower's stated income. The ethical action is to:
options: Ignore it to keep the file moving
Ask the borrower to source and document the deposit and convey the material information to the underwriter
Delete the deposit from the statements
Coach the borrower to call it a gift regardless of the facts
questions.explanation: A large unexplained deposit is material; it may be an undisclosed loan affecting DTI or another underwriting concern. The MLO must have the borrower source and document it and must convey the material information to the underwriter. Ignoring, altering statements, or coaching a false explanation is fraud.
questions.primary_source_citation: SAFE Act prohibited acts, 12 CFR §1008.103; duty of accurate disclosure to lender/underwriter

questions.stem: Which action regarding the appraisal is permissible for an MLO?
options: Telling the appraiser the value the deal needs to reach
Providing the appraiser with factual information such as the purchase contract
Choosing an appraiser known to return high values
Withholding payment unless the value comes in high enough
questions.explanation: Appraiser-independence rules prohibit coercing, influencing, or pressuring an appraiser toward a target value. Supplying legitimate factual information, such as the sales contract, is permitted. Communicating a needed value, selecting appraisers for inflated results, or conditioning payment on the outcome are all prohibited.
questions.primary_source_citation: Regulation Z, 12 CFR §1026.42 (valuation independence)

questions.stem: Under the SAFE Act, the minimum pre-licensing education and the minimum annual continuing education for a state-licensed MLO are:
options: 20 hours pre-licensing; 8 hours CE per year
8 hours pre-licensing; 20 hours CE per year
40 hours pre-licensing; 12 hours CE per year
20 hours pre-licensing; no CE required
questions.explanation: The SAFE Act requires a minimum of 20 hours of NMLS-approved pre-licensing education and at least 8 hours of NMLS-approved continuing education each year. States may require additional hours but not fewer, and CE is not optional for maintaining a license.

questions.subtopic: SAFE Act — Regulation G vs H
questions.stem: Regulation H under the SAFE Act applies to:
options: Employees of depository institutions (registered MLOs)
Nondepository institutions and their employees, such as state-licensed mortgage companies, brokers, and MLOs
Only federal credit unions
Appraisers
questions.explanation: Regulation H governs state licensing of nondepository institutions and their loan originators. Regulation G covers federal registration of MLOs employed by depository institutions. The distinction between registered (depository, Reg G) and licensed (nondepository, Reg H) originators is a common Uniform State item.
questions.primary_source_citation: Regulation G, 12 CFR Part 1007; Regulation H, 12 CFR Part 1008

questions.stem: How does a felony conviction affect MLO licensing eligibility under the SAFE Act?
options: It has no effect
A felony in the past 7 years bars licensing; a felony involving fraud, dishonesty, breach of trust, or money laundering bars licensing permanently
It matters only for misdemeanors
It bars licensing for 30 days
questions.explanation: The SAFE Act permanently bars anyone convicted at any time of a felony involving fraud, dishonesty, breach of trust, or money laundering, and bars licensing for any felony conviction within the preceding seven years. Fingerprint-based background checks enforce these standards.
